🚀 WE’RE HIRING: MECHANICAL DESIGN ENGINEER — SEMICONDUCTOR & VACUUM HARDWARE
Design complex CNC-machined parts and explain how you’d put them into production.
We’re looking for a senior mechanical design engineer to create original CAD packages for semiconductor equipment and vacuum hardware.
📍 Role details
• 🌍 Global | Fully remote
• Contract type: Contractor
• Compensation: $90–$155 per hour
• Payment schedule: Unspecified
• Project scope: Initial phase of 20 part packages, followed by production
💡 The opportunity
• Design parts from scratch around specific machining challenges. Each package receives three independent engineering reviews. No prior AI experience is required.
📋 What you’ll do
• Deliver native parametric CAD files, STEP files, and production drawings with full GD&T, datums, material specifications, and finishes.
• Document each part’s function, interfaces, operating conditions, and the reasoning behind material and process choices.
• Justify estimates for unit cost, CNC cycle and setup times, production volume, sourcing difficulty, and lead time.
• Review peer submissions for technical quality and production feasibility, then revise your own packages based on feedback.
🎯 What you’ll bring

The conversation around AWS in 2026 has shifted from "which instance type is fastest" to something far more strategic: how we design a multi-account architecture that survives the velocity of AI-driven provisioning without losing control of data or cost.

The quiet but critical announcement at this year's re:Invent was the maturation of AWS Control Tower as a policy enforcement engine, not just an account factory. The new capabilities let you define governance rules at the organizational unit level—cost boundaries, data residency requirements, compliance baselines—and inject them into every provisioning request automatically. This collapses the gap between what finance wants and what engineering builds.

The non-obvious implication is what this means for the engineer's role. Most teams have approached multi-account management as a set of account templates and manual guardrails. The new approach treats every account request as a policy event. The platform engineer no longer configures accounts. They design the policy model that accounts must obey. The developer requests a sandbox. Control Tower enforces the data classification, the encryption standard, and the budget cap without any human intervention.

The second thread is the quiet evolution of cost anomaly detection into a governance primitive. What was once a simple alerting system is now a policy enforcement mechanism. You can define a rule that says, "If spend on any single service exceeds 20% of forecast for two consecutive hours, the provisioning pipeline is paused until a human reviews the plan." This is not monitoring. It is a safety guarantee for autonomous operations.

For hiring managers, the AWS specialist of 2026 is not the engineer who can optimize a single account's reserved instances. It is the engineer who can design the account governance model that survives the scale of AI-driven provisioning without breaking compliance or budget. They understand that every account is a policy container, every cost event is a governance signal, and every Terraform plan is a contract between the operator and the organization.

The talent gap is acute. Most teams can manage a handful of accounts. Very few can design a multi-account architecture where policy is the first-class primitive and provisioning is just the execution of that policy.

How are you embedding policy enforcement into every stage of your AWS multi-account lifecycle, from account creation to decommissioning, when the operator is an AI agent?

Public procurement is becoming more digital. But is it becoming more economically accessible to SMEs?

This week, TED-together 2026 brought renewed attention to procurement data quality, transparency, interoperability and AI-assisted validation.
These are important developments.
But having managed a general contracting business, I believe there's another problem that deserves considerably more attention.

The real challenge for small and medium-sized enterprises isn't simply finding a tender. It's determining whether winning that tender will actually make financial sense.

Consider what happens before a company even submits its bid.

Technical documentation must be reviewed. Market prices must be checked. Suppliers and delivery schedules must be evaluated. Contractual obligations and financial risks must be assessed.
And someone has to do all this work.

For an SME, this often means hiring specialists or paying external consultants to prepare the bid, evaluate risks and support the contract throughout its execution.
These expenses don't disappear when the contract is awarded.
Add procurement costs, logistics, financing, potential delays, contractual penalties and taxes.

How much profit is actually left?

Sometimes, surprisingly little.
And sometimes the apparent profitability of a contract disappears entirely once its real costs are calculated.

This is precisely the problem I want to address with TenderCore Europe, the fully open-source procurement intelligence platform I'm developing.

My goal isn't to build another tender search engine.
It's to create an instrument that helps businesses understand the economics of a potential contract before committing resources.

A system designed to analyze procurement conditions, estimate commercial viability, identify potential hidden costs and highlight operational and contractual risks.
In other words, to reveal as many of the potential pitfalls as possible before they become expensive problems.

AI and structured procurement data can help make this type of analysis more accessible, particularly to businesses that cannot afford dedicated procurement, legal and financial departments.

Of course, no software can eliminate every commercial risk or replace professional judgment.
But it can help entrepreneurs make better-informed decisions.

I believe the next stage of procurement digitalization shouldn't be measured only by how easily businesses can find opportunities.

It should also be measured by how effectively they can determine which opportunities are actually worth pursuing.

Because winning a contract and making money from it are two very different achievements.

I built an AI resume screener that reads PDFs and Word files, then ranks candidates against a job description.

Not with a black-box tool. With a plain Python pipeline where every step is typed and inspectable. 👇

The pipeline
1. Job description -> LLM -> a validated JobD object (role, required skills, preferred skills, minimum experience, education, responsibilities)
2. Resume (PDF via pypdf, DOCX via python-docx, including tables) -> LLM -> a validated Resume object (skills, experiences, education, projects, certifications)
3. JobD + Resume -> LLM -> a MatchResult (score 0-100, matching skills, missing skills, verdict)
4. Sort by score -> print the top 2 and lowest 2 candidates

I tested it on a real Amazon SDE-I job description against a folder of resumes.

What made it work
- Pydantic schemas as contracts. If the model returns the wrong shape, it fails loudly instead of silently corrupting data.
- JSON mode + a prompt that says: do not invent information, return null if missing.
- Parsing by meaning, not headings. "Work History", "Employment" and "Internships" all land in the same field.
- Two small LLM calls (parse, then score) instead of one giant prompt. Easier to debug, easier to improve.

What I'd be careful about
LLM scores are not objective. Same resume, different run, slightly different number. This should shortlist and explain, never reject people on its own. A human stays in the loop.

Next improvements: deterministic skill matching to anchor the score, a scoring rubric in the prompt, and a simple UI.

If you work in hiring or HR tech: what would make a tool like this trustworthy enough to use?

🚀 API Testing with GraphQL — A Practical Cheat Sheet for QA Engineers

If you're moving from REST API testing to GraphQL, one of the biggest mindset changes is this:

👉 REST exposes multiple endpoints.
👉 GraphQL usually gives you one endpoint, and the client specifies exactly what data it needs.

But how do you actually test it? 🤔

Here’s a quick breakdown.
🔹 1. Understand the GraphQL Schema
Before writing tests, understand:
• Types
• Fields
• Relationships
• Queries
• Mutations
• Arguments
• Resolvers
The schema is your contract.

🔹 2. Test Queries
Verify that:
✅ Valid queries return the expected data
✅ Required fields are enforced
✅ Invalid fields return proper errors
✅ Nested objects work correctly
✅ Optional fields behave correctly
✅ Pagination, filtering & sorting work as expected

🔹 3. Test Mutations
Don't test only the happy path.
Test:
✅ Create
✅ Update
✅ Delete
✅ Invalid input
✅ Missing required fields
✅ Duplicate data
✅ Authorization
✅ Business validations

🔹 4. Validate the Response
Check more than HTTP status.
Validate:
• Response structure
• Returned fields
• Data types
• Nullability
• Error messages
• Partial responses
• Business rules

🔹 5. Don't Forget Security 🔐
GraphQL testing should include:
🚨 Authentication
🚨 Authorization
🚨 IDOR / access-control testing
🚨 Query depth limits
🚨 Query complexity
🚨 Rate limiting
🚨 Sensitive field exposure

🔹 6. Test GraphQL Errors
A successful HTTP response doesn't always mean the GraphQL operation succeeded.

Your automation should validate the errors section as well as the data section.
🧪 QA Mindset

Think beyond:
"Does the API return 200?"
Instead ask:
"Did the API return the right data, for the right user, under the right conditions?"
That's where real API testing begins.

📌 Save this cheat sheet if you're learning GraphQL or preparing for QA/SDET interviews.

Ai projects advertise 52% bigger budgets. But it's not because of the "AI" label. 👇

New OpenAI x Upwork research compared AI-related freelance projects with similar non-AI ones:

→ Advertised fixed-price budgets: 52% higher
→ Advertised hourly rates: only 1.5% higher
→ Hours logged in the first 90 days of hourly contracts: 41% more

what this tells me: clients aren't paying a premium for AI skills alone. they're hiring for bigger, connected projects, where one freelancer delivers the whole outcome.

as a WordPress developer, I see the same thing. A website is rarely just a design. It's design + build + speed + SEO + the custom features that make it work for the business. I use AI-assisted development (Claude Code) to deliver that faster, and I review and test everything before it goes live.

One caveat: the study covers Upwork postings only, and it doesn't prove freelancers earn more. But the direction is clear. The value is in delivering complete outcomes, not just using AI tools.

If you hire freelancers: do you want the design only, or the whole outcome? 👇

Peter Wong, P.Eng. — AI Engineer | Agentic AI Consulting
Toronto, Ontario · petercmwong@gmail.com · +1 647-993-2765
github.com/peterwong7
Dear Hiring Team,
I am a licensed Professional Engineer in Ontario with four decades of engineering and technology leadership, now building hands-on AI systems — and I am writing to introduce myself to Toronto firms putting AI to work, in financial services, insurance, and beyond.
For twenty years I was an Application Portfolio Manager at one of Canada's largest banks, leading a team of project managers and business analysts, governing a portfolio of applications, and setting technology direction. Before that, I led consulting engagements as a manager with Vignette Corporation and with the City of Toronto's Public Health division, and held engineering roles with CIBC, Aetna, IBM, and the University of Toronto. I know how large organizations assess technology, manage risk, and adopt new systems — because I have done it from the inside.
This year I retrained in AI and completed Harvard's CS50P and CS50AI with certificates. My portfolio is public on GitHub: a retrieval-augmented chatbot, a multi-step AI agent that plans and uses tools to complete goals, and a failure-mode checker that audits AI answers for unsupported claims and contradictions. That last one reflects my specialty — seeing where AI systems can fail before they do, and building the checks that catch it.
I am available for AI engineering and agentic AI consulting engagements, contract or project-based, remote or in Toronto. If your firm is building AI systems that have to work safely in the real world, I would welcome a conversation.
Yours truly,
Peter Wong, P.Eng.
